title: Conspiracy Factual Impossibility
subject: Criminal Law & Procedure
subtopic: Inchoate Crimes - conspiracy and factual impossibility
stem: At trial, Paul and Rebekah move to dismiss a charge of conspiracy to receive and resell stolen property. Weeks earlier, they had agreed to buy several irrigation controllers from a seller who said the controllers had been stolen from a nearby orchard. They planned to resell them to small farms. The seller was an undercover officer, and the controllers were police-created props that had never been stolen.
call: Should the motion be granted on the ground that the controllers were not actually stolen?

choices.A: No, because they agreed to obtain and resell property they believed was stolen.
choices.B: No, but only because irrigation controllers are serial-numbered farm equipment.
choices.C: Yes, because the irrigation controllers were not in fact stolen.
choices.D: Yes, because conspiracy requires completion of the planned receiving offense.

rightExplanation: Conspiracy punishes the agreement to commit a crime plus the required intent. Factual impossibility is generally not a defense when the defendants agreed to conduct that would have been criminal if the facts were as they believed. Paul and Rebekah believed the controllers were stolen and agreed to buy and resell them on that basis. The fact that the items were police-created props defeats the completed receiving offense, but it does not defeat the conspiracy charge.

wrongExplanations.C: The absence of actually stolen property feels decisive because the target offense could not be completed. The breaker is that factual impossibility does not bar conspiracy when the agreed facts would make the conduct criminal.
wrongExplanations.D: The completed-offense requirement sounds plausible because receiving stolen property needs stolen property. Conspiracy is complete upon the unlawful agreement and required intent; the object offense need not be completed.
wrongExplanations.B: This reaches the right result but for a limiting reason the law does not require. The same impossibility rule applies without regard to serial numbers or the farm-equipment character of the property.
